arml-1996-power-01a.title: Induction
arml-1996-power-01a.body: Claim: $L_n$ begins with $1,n$. True for $L_1=(1,1)$. If $L_n$ begins $1,n,\dots$, then $L_{n+1}$ begins $1,\ 1+n,\ n,\dots$, i.e. it begins $1,n+1$. So the integer $n$ appears in $L_n$ for every $n\ge1$. ∎

arml-1996-power-01b.title: Track the 13s
arml-1996-power-01b.body:
A $13$ is created in $L_{m+1}$ exactly when two consecutive terms $a,13-a$ of $L_m$ are summed, and once present it stays in all later lists. By problems 7 and 8 below, an ordered pair $(a,b)$ is consecutive in exactly one list when $a,b$ are coprime, and that list is found by running the subtractive Euclidean algorithm backwards: if $k$ subtractions take $(a,b)$ to $(1,1)$, the pair is consecutive in $L_{k+1}$ and the sum $a+b$ is inserted in $L_{k+2}$.

The $12$ ordered pairs $(a,13-a)$, $a=1,\dots,12$ (all coprime to $13$), give:

| pair | $(5,8),(8,5)$ | $(3,10),(4,9),(9,4),(10,3)$ | $(2,11),(6,7),(7,6),(11,2)$ | $(1,12),(12,1)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| subtractions $k$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ | $11$ |
| first appears in $L_{k+2}$ | $L_6$ | $L_7$ | $L_8$ | $L_{13}$ |

So $H(n)$ is the number of the $12$ occurrences already present: $H(2)=0$; $H(6)=2$; $H(7)=6$; $H(8)=\dots=H(12)=10$; $H(n)=12$ for all $n\ge13$, in particular $H(100)=12$. (Check: $L_6$ above contains exactly two $13$s.)

**Answer: $H(2)=0$, $H(6)=2$, $H(10)=10$, $H(12)=10$, $H(100)=12$**

arml-1996-power-02a.title: Formulas for each position
arml-1996-power-02a.body:
Each list begins with the first terms of the previous list, interleaved with their sums. Starting from $L_{1993}$, which begins $1,1993,\dots$:

- $L_{1994}$ begins $1,\ 1994,\ 1993,\dots$
- $L_{1995}$ begins $1,\ 1995,\ 1994,\ 3987,\ 1993,\dots$
- $L_{1996}$ begins $1,\ 1996,\ 1995,\ 3989,\ 1994,\ 5981,\ 3987,\dots$

(Equivalently, the first seven terms of $L_n$ are $1,\,n,\,n-1,\,2n-3,\,n-2,\,3n-7,\,2n-5$.)

**Answer: $1,1996,1995,3989,1994,5981,3987$**

arml-1996-power-02b.title: Go backwards
arml-1996-power-02b.body:
Each term of $L_n$ is either an old term of $L_{n-1}$ or the sum of two neighbouring old terms. Since $8<1995$, the term $1995$ is a sum $8+1987$ and $8$ is an old term; similarly $1997=8+1989$. So $1987,8,1989$ are consecutive in $L_{n-1}$. Repeating, $1979,8,1981$ in $L_{n-2}$, and so on: after $k$ steps we have $1995-8k,\,8,\,1997-8k$. After $k=249$ steps: $3,8,5$ consecutive in $L_{n-249}$. The triple $3,8,5$ first appears in $L_5=1,5,4,7,3,8,5,\dots$ (and by problem 8 a pair of consecutive numbers occurs in only one list), so $n-249=5$, $n=254$.

**Answer: 254**

arml-1996-power-03.title: Induction
arml-1996-power-03.body:
Let $f(n)$ be the number of terms. $f(1)=2=2^0+1$. $L_n$ has $f(n)-1$ gaps between consecutive terms, and $L_{n+1}$ has one new term in each: $f(n+1)=f(n)+f(n)-1$. If $f(n)=2^{n-1}+1$, then $f(n+1)=2(2^{n-1}+1)-1=2^n+1$. ∎

**Answer: $2^{n-1}+1$**

arml-1996-power-04.title: Sum of the terms
arml-1996-power-04.body:
Let $s(n)$ be the sum of the terms of $L_n$: $s(1)=2$. $L_{n+1}$ consists of the terms of $L_n$ together with the sums of neighbouring pairs; every term of $L_n$ except the first and last is used in two such sums, and the two end terms in one each. So the new terms sum to $2s(n)-2$ (the ends are $1+1=2$), and $s(n+1)=s(n)+2s(n)-2=3s(n)-2$. With $s(1)=2=3^0+1$ and $s(n)=3^{n-1}+1$: $s(n+1)=3(3^{n-1}+1)-2=3^n+1$. ∎

With $2^{n-1}+1$ terms (problem 3), the average is $\dfrac{3^{n-1}+1}{2^{n-1}+1}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{3^{n-1}+1}{2^{n-1}+1}$**

arml-1996-power-06a.title: Induction
arml-1996-power-06a.body:
Claim: in $L_n$, every term is at most $F_{n+1}$, every two consecutive terms sum to at most $F_{n+2}$, and $F_n,F_{n+1}$ are consecutive.

For $L_1=(1,1)$ this holds. Assume it for $L_n$. The terms of $L_{n+1}$ are old terms (at most $F_{n+1}\le F_{n+2}$) and sums $a+b$ of consecutive old terms (at most $F_{n+2}$), so every term is at most $F_{n+2}$. Consecutive terms of $L_{n+1}$ have the form $a,\ a+b$ or $a+b,\ b$ with $a,b$ consecutive in $L_n$, with sum $(a+b)+a\le F_{n+2}+F_{n+1}=F_{n+3}$ or $(a+b)+b\le F_{n+3}$. Finally, the consecutive pair $F_n,F_{n+1}$ in $L_n$ produces the new term $F_{n+2}$ next to $F_{n+1}$. So the claim holds for $L_{n+1}$, and $F_{n+1}$ is the largest term of $L_n$. ∎

arml-1996-power-06b.title: Largest-element bound
arml-1996-power-06b.body:
By part (a) the largest term of $L_n$ is $F_{n+1}$. The Fibonacci numbers are $\dots,987,1597,2584,\dots$, with $F_{17}=1597<1996<2584=F_{18}$. So $1996$ cannot appear in $L_{16}$ (largest term $1597$) or any earlier list, and it could possibly appear in $L_{17}$ (largest term $2584$). So the least possible value of $n$ is $17$.

(In fact a direct computation shows that $1996$ first appears in $L_{18}$, as $741+1255$ and $765+1231$; the bound $17$ is what the problem asks for.)

**Answer: 17**

arml-1996-power-07.title: Euclid step
arml-1996-power-07.body: Induction on $n$. $L_1=(1,1)$ is fine. In $L_{n+1}$, two consecutive terms are an old term $b$ and a new term $a=b+c$ where $c$ is the old neighbour (consecutive with $b$ in $L_n$). Then $\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(b+c,b)=\gcd(c,b)=1$ by the induction hypothesis. ∎

arml-1996-power-08.title: Backward uniqueness
arml-1996-power-08.body: If $a>b$ are consecutive (in either order) in $L_n$, $n\ge2$, then the larger is a new term, so in $L_{n-1}$ the consecutive terms are $a-b$ and $b$ (in the same relative order). Repeating this subtracts the smaller from the larger each time (the subtractive Euclidean algorithm) and is completely determined by $(a,b)$ and their order; it ends at $(1,1)$ in $L_1$ after a definite number of steps. If $(a,b)$ were consecutive in $L_n$ and in $L_m$, both backward chains would be the same, so the number of steps to reach $L_1$, namely $n-1$ and $m-1$, would be equal: $n=m$. ∎

arml-1996-power-09.title: Count coprime neighbours
arml-1996-power-09.body:
Every occurrence of $t\ge2$ in a list $L_n$ ($n\ge2$) is the sum of two consecutive terms of an earlier list, or an older occurrence. Each such sum is $a+b$ with $a,b$ consecutive, hence coprime (problem 7), $a+b=t$, and by problem 8 each ordered pair $(a,b)$ is consecutive in at most one list. Conversely, every ordered pair $(a,b)$ of coprime positive integers is consecutive in some list: induct on $a+b$ — for $(1,1)$ this is $L_1$, and if $a>b$ the pair $(a-b,b)$ is coprime with smaller sum, so it is consecutive in some $L_m$, and then $(a,b)$ is consecutive in $L_{m+1}$ (similarly for $a<b$).

So the occurrences of $t$ in all lists correspond to the ordered pairs $(a,t-a)$ with $1\le a\le t-1$ and $\gcd(a,t)=1$: exactly $\varphi(t)$ of them, and they are all present in a late enough list. Hence the maximum of $N(t)$ is $\varphi(t)$. For $t=1996=2^2\cdot499$: $\varphi(1996)=1996\left(1-\frac12\right)\left(1-\frac1{499}\right)=998\cdot\frac{498}{499}=996$.

**Answer: 996**

arml-1996-power-10.title: Count even terms recursively
arml-1996-power-10.body:
Let $e_n$ be the number of even terms in $L_n$; $L_n$ has $2^{n-1}+1$ terms (problem 3).

*No two even terms are adjacent*, since consecutive terms are coprime (problem 7). Also the end terms are $1$ (odd). So each even term has two odd neighbours, and the number of consecutive pairs containing an even term is exactly $2e_n$. The number of pairs of consecutive terms is $2^{n-1}$, so the number of (odd, odd) pairs is $2^{n-1}-2e_n$.

The new terms of $L_{n+1}$ are even exactly for (odd, odd) pairs. So $e_{n+1}=e_n+(2^{n-1}-2e_n)=2^{n-1}-e_n$, with $e_1=0$.

Claim $e_n=\frac{2^{n-1}+(-1)^n}3$. True for $n=1$ ($\frac{1-1}{3}=0$). If true for $n$, then $e_{n+1}=2^{n-1}-\frac{2^{n-1}+(-1)^n}3=\frac{2^n-(-1)^n}3=\frac{2^n+(-1)^{n+1}}3$ ✓.

For even $n$, $e_n=\frac{2^{n-1}+1}3$, which is exactly one third of the $2^{n-1}+1$ terms; hence the odd terms number $2e_n$. ∎
